newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal underlines claim to EMU place.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal underlines claim to EMU place.

text.p: Portugal's Socialist government on Friday sought to strengthen its bid to be amongst the founders of the single currency with a rigorous economic plan to halve the budget deficit by the millenium.

In what was aimed as a clear rebuttal to those that charge Portugal's financial effort cannot be maintained, the government said that "sustainability" would be the cornerstone of its 1998-2000 programme.

"The sustainability of the process...constitutes an overriding objective," the Finance Ministry said, presenting the 'Programme for Convergence, Stability and Growth' which was sent to the European Commission on Friday.

Portugal, which has set its sights on securing a place in the vanguard of European Union countries to launch economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, is widely expected to pass most of the economic tests for entry.
Local economists expect the government to meet its target of a budget deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, just inside the three percent EMU threshhold.

The country also received some good news on the inflation front on Friday with the year-on-year rate slipping to 2.9 percent in February, from 3.3 percent the month before, taking the government closer to its end-year target of 2.5 percent.
Inflation has often been cited as Portugal's biggest challenge on the road to monetary union.

Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco reaffirmed the government's confidence in making the grade, telling a news conference that the programme looked toward "Portugal being amongst the founders...something which we believe."

But questions have been raised, particularly in northern Europe, about whether the great financial effort being made by southern partners such as Portugal in the name of EMU membership can be kept up over time.

The reply from the Portuguese finance ministry was that it believed the drive for budgetary discipline and lower inflation was not only vital for EMU, it was crucial to economic success in or out of the single currency.

"The rigour and discipline of budgetary policy constitute... the pillar of macro-economic stability...indispensable to consolidate the confidence of markets and encourage non-inflationary growth," it said in its introduction to the programme.
The plan sees the budget deficit in 2000 narrowing to just 1.5 percent of the country's total economic output as measured by GDP. Inflation would be reduced to a miserly 1.8 percent.
But some commentators have warned that these sort of goals may be too tough for an emerging economy like that of Portugal, one of the European Union's poorest members.
"It might be alright for Germany -- (but) it is too aggressive for a fragile economy like ours," wrote the Diario Economico financial daily in an editorial on Friday.
